From the surgery

A ten-minute appointment

Time in primary care is short. Some simple ideas to make better use of it, especially when what worries you is how you are feeling.

By Alejandro Rosàs, family doctor

Primary care appointments usually last between five and ten minutes. That is little time to talk about something as complex as mood, anxiety or grief, and many people leave feeling they have not said what mattered. A few ideas can help both patient and doctor make better use of it.

Before you go

  • Write down what you want to discuss, in order of importance. If there are several things, start with what worries you most.
  • Note since when it has been happening, how it has changed and what makes it worse or better.
  • Bring a list of your medicines, including over-the-counter ones, herbal remedies and supplements.
  • If it is hard to talk about, you can bring it in writing and hand it to the doctor.

During the appointment

  • Say at the start that you want to talk about your mood or nerves, not at the end.
  • Ask about anything you do not understand and repeat in your own words what has been explained.
  • Ask what happens next: whether you need to come back, when and what to do if things get worse.
  • If you need to, ask for a longer appointment or a scheduled one to talk calmly. Many surgeries offer this.

Afterwards

It is normal to forget part of what is said in the appointment, especially when nervous. Writing down the advice or bringing someone with you helps. And if something was not clear, you can ask again.

The relationship with a family doctor is one of the few in healthcare that lasts for years. That continuity is valuable: it allows the doctor to know the person, their history and their surroundings, and that is also a therapeutic tool.
